title: FreshRoute - cold-chain monitoring for food distributors
pitch_text: FreshRoute provides temperature monitoring and route alerts for small food distributors operating refrigerated vans. A wireless sensor is placed inside each vehicle and sends temperature readings to a cloud dashboard every two minutes. If temperature moves outside a customer-defined range, the driver and dispatcher receive an alert. The service costs 35 EUR per vehicle per month plus a one-off 90 EUR sensor fee. FreshRoute completed a four-month pilot with three regional distributors covering 72 vans. The company reports that temperature-related delivery rejections fell from 19 incidents in the four months before the pilot to 7 incidents during the pilot. It currently has 58 paying vehicles after the pilot, generating 2,030 EUR in monthly subscription revenue. Sensor connectivity and cloud data transfer cost approximately 3.20 EUR per active vehicle per month, while the pitch does not state sensor manufacturing cost, installation cost or customer-support cost. The founding team includes an embedded-systems engineer, a logistics manager and a part-time salesperson. FreshRoute plans to reach 1,000 subscribed vehicles across Italy and Slovenia within 24 months and is raising 350,000 EUR to finance inventory, hire two salespeople and improve the dashboard. Customer acquisition currently depends on referrals from refrigeration-repair workshops. The pitch names large fleet-management platforms as indirect competitors but argues that these products are broader and more expensive than FreshRoute's focused monitoring service.
notes: Main-study synthetic pitch. IoT/SaaS with measurable pilot evidence, variable cost and channel dependency.

title: CareQueue - scheduling optimisation for private clinics
pitch_text: CareQueue is a software platform for small private clinics that predicts appointment no-shows and automatically offers cancelled time slots to patients on a waiting list. Clinics connect their existing appointment calendar to CareQueue through an integration provided during onboarding. The platform charges 220 EUR per clinic per month with no setup fee. A six-month pilot involved 12 clinics with a combined 18,400 scheduled appointments. The founders report that unused appointment slots fell by 14 percent during the pilot and that 9 of the 12 clinics converted to paid subscriptions afterward. Current monthly recurring revenue is therefore 1,980 EUR. The pitch does not provide the clinics' previous no-show rate, the number of recovered appointments or the monetary value of recovered capacity. CareQueue uses a machine-learning model trained on scheduling history and basic appointment metadata, but the pitch does not describe model accuracy, data-retention arrangements or how performance differs between clinics. The team includes a data scientist, a full-stack developer and a former clinic administrator. Sales are currently founder-led through direct outreach to clinic owners. CareQueue aims to sign 150 clinics in Spain within 18 months and is raising 500,000 EUR to hire two sales staff, one integration engineer and fund compliance work. The pitch identifies established clinic-management software vendors as competitors but argues that most focus on administration rather than predictive scheduling.
notes: Main-study synthetic pitch. B2B healthcare software with conversion data, integration/privacy questions and incomplete value quantification.

title: BuildFlow - procurement marketplace for construction sites
pitch_text: BuildFlow is a digital procurement platform for small and medium-sized construction contractors. Site managers upload a list of required materials, and local suppliers submit quotes through the platform. BuildFlow earns a 3 percent transaction fee on completed orders and does not charge contractors a subscription. The company ran a five-month pilot with 24 contractors and 38 suppliers. During the pilot, 410 orders with a total gross merchandise value of 286,000 EUR were completed through the platform. BuildFlow therefore generated approximately 8,580 EUR in transaction-fee revenue during the pilot. The founders report that contractors received an average of 3.4 supplier quotes per order and that quoted prices differed by an average of 11 percent between the lowest and highest offer. No data is provided on repeat-order rates, payment failures, supplier churn or the cost of acquiring contractors and suppliers. Payments are processed by a third-party payment provider, while BuildFlow coordinates order status but does not store or deliver materials. The team consists of a former construction project manager, a software developer and a commercial lead. BuildFlow plans to expand from one metropolitan area to four cities within 18 months and is seeking 450,000 EUR to hire sales staff and add supplier-management features. The pitch states that contractors currently source materials through phone calls, messaging apps and existing supplier relationships, which BuildFlow views as its main alternative.
notes: Main-study synthetic pitch. Two-sided marketplace with transaction economics, network effects and retention uncertainty.

title: ChargeNest - shared EV charging management for apartment buildings
pitch_text: ChargeNest provides software and metering hardware that allows apartment buildings to share a limited number of electric-vehicle charging points among residents. Residents reserve charging slots in a mobile app, and the system records electricity consumption for monthly billing by the property manager. ChargeNest charges the building 12 EUR per active charging user per month and sells each connected meter for 140 EUR. A nine-month pilot was installed in eight apartment buildings with 96 registered EV drivers, of whom 74 used the system in the most recent month. The pitch reports 888 EUR in monthly subscription revenue from those active users and states that 87 percent of charging sessions were completed within the reserved time window. Hardware manufacturing costs 62 EUR per meter, but installation, maintenance, payment-processing and customer-support costs are not provided. The software is hosted in the cloud and communicates with meters through an external connectivity provider. The team consists of an electrical engineer, a software engineer and a property-management consultant. ChargeNest plans to reach 1,500 active users across 80 buildings in Germany within two years and is raising 700,000 EUR for hardware inventory, certification, installation partners and two sales hires. The pitch identifies dedicated home chargers and building-wide charging-system vendors as alternatives, while claiming that ChargeNest is easier to deploy in buildings with limited electrical capacity.
notes: Main-study synthetic pitch. Hardware plus SaaS with explicit unit cost, operational dependencies and scaling target.
